html:
The Tashkent earthquake of 26 April 1966 was fairly small, with a magnitude of 5.2, but its centre lay just a few kilometres under the middle of Tashkent, capital of Soviet Uzbekistan.

Most of the old city's mud brick houses collapsed. Between 15 and 200 people died, but up to 300,000 were left homeless.

The Soviet government made the rebuilding a show of the "friendship of peoples". Building teams came from every Soviet republic, and each put up its own district. Old Tashkent, with its winding lanes, gave way to wide avenues, concrete apartment blocks and modernist public buildings, many decorated with mosaics. The new city got the first metro in Central Asia, the Tashkent Metro, in 1977. A monument to the courage of the people marks the spot above the quake's centre. It shaped the city that Russia had taken a century before into a Soviet model capital.
